question: A Dynamo-style store has N = 5 and W = 3. What is the smallest R that makes every read quorum overlap every write quorum?
explanation: Overlap needs R + W > N, so R > 2 and the smallest value is 3. R = 2 gives R + W = N, so a read can hit only the two replicas the write missed.

question: With N = 5, R = 2, W = 4, how many replicas can be down while reads still answer, and while writes still succeed?
options: reads survive 2 down, writes survive 4 down
reads survive 1 down, writes survive 3 down
reads survive 3 down, writes survive 3 down
reads survive 3 down, writes survive 1 down
explanation: A read needs R live replicas (5 - 2 = 3 may fail) and a write needs W (5 - 4 = 1 may fail). Large W buys fresher reads at the price of write availability, the PC side of PACELC.

question: N = 3, R = 2, W = 2 showed 0% stale reads but 2 inversions under a slow-message tail. Why is R + W > N not enough for linearizability?
options: It only holds when every replica is in the same region
It prevents stale reads of finished writes, not new-then-old reads during an in-flight write
Inversions come from clock skew, which quorums cannot see
R + W > N is only a liveness rule; it says nothing at all about which value a read returns to clients
explanation: While a write has reached only some replicas, one read quorum can include the new value and a later one can miss it. Read write-back (store the newest value on W replicas before returning) closes that gap.

question: N = 3, R = 2, W = 2. A write has reached replica a only. Reader 1 asks a and b; reader 2 starts after reader 1 finishes and asks b and c. What do they return?
options: Reader 1 the new value, reader 2 the old one: not linearizable
Both return the new value, because R + W > N
Both return the old value, because the write has not finished
Reader 2 blocks until the write reaches a majority
explanation: Reader 1 sees the new version on a; reader 2's quorum {b, c} has only the old one, so values go backwards between two non-overlapping reads. It can still be sequentially consistent, but not linearizable.

question: Why did read write-back barely change read p50 but nearly double read p99 (65.9 to 124.5 ms)?
options: It runs on every read, but most reads hit a replica in the local zone, which hides its cost
It only runs when the R replies disagree, which happens mostly in the tail
It replaces the second replica's reply with a slower region
It waits for all N replicas instead of R
explanation: The extra write phase is needed only when replies differ, mostly while a write is in flight or delayed, so typical reads are unaffected. Keep write-back for keys that need linearizability.

question: Clients are partitioned so only replica a is reachable. With R = 1, W = 3, what share of reads and writes are answered?
options: Reads 0%, writes 100%
Reads 100%, writes 100%
Reads 0%, writes 0%
Reads 100%, writes 0%
explanation: A read needs one replica, which is reachable; a write needs all three acknowledgements, which it cannot get. R = 3, W = 1 is the mirror image, and R = 2, W = 2 refuses both.

question: One store holds a cart badge (≤20% stale, fast), feature flags (≤1% stale, read-your-writes) and a lock-owner key (linearizable). Which assignment did the lab's measurements support?
options: Cart R=2 W=2; flags R=1 W=1; lock R=3 W=1, the only linearizable choice
All three R=2 W=2, since it has 0% stale reads
Cart R=1 W=1; flags R=2 W=2; lock R=2 W=2 plus read write-back
All three R=1 W=1, since partitions are rare
explanation: Each use case gets the fastest setting that meets its constraints: R=1 W=1 is fine for a badge, R=2 W=2 for flags, and only write-back makes the lock linearizable while surviving region C's loss. R=3 W=1 is linearizable but answers 0% with C down.

question: Finished reads of a single-writer register are scanned for inversions (a read older than an already finished read). What is printed?
explanation: The read at [6, 9] returned version 1 after the read at [0, 5] had already returned version 2, which is one inversion; the read at [10, 12] returning 2 is fine. Overlapping reads would not count.

question: A G-Counter merge is applied, and the laptop's state is delivered twice. What is printed?
explanation: Merge takes the per-slot max, so phone=3 and laptop=2 give 5, and merging the same state again changes nothing. A sum-based merge would double-count the duplicate.

question: A PN-Counter has increments P = {a: 7, b: 4} and decrements N = {a: 2, b: 3}. What is its value?
explanation: The value is sum(P) - sum(N) = 11 - 5. Each side is a G-Counter, so both stay monotone and merge by per-slot max.

question: Two replicas that assigned the title at the same Lamport timestamp never agree after syncing. What is the fix?
options: Order by (timestamp, replica id) so every replica picks the same winner
Use wall-clock time instead of Lamport timestamps
Change > to >= so that the incoming value always wins when the timestamps are equal
Sync more often so ties cannot happen
explanation: On a tie each side keeps its own value, so merge(x, y) != merge(y, x); a total order on (timestamp, replica id) makes it commutative. '>=' still diverges, because each side then takes the other's value.

question: The phone removes milk while the laptop concurrently re-adds it; the OR-Set states are then merged. What is printed?
code:
a_tags, a_tomb = {"t1"}, set()  # phone
b_tags, b_tomb = {"t1"}, set()  # laptop
a_tomb |= a_tags                  # phone removes milk (saw t1)
b_tags = b_tags | {"t2"}          # laptop re-adds milk concurrently
tags, tomb = a_tags | b_tags, a_tomb | b_tomb
print(sorted(tags - tomb))
explanation: The phone's remove tombstones only the tag it saw (t1); the laptop's new tag t2 was never observed, so it survives and milk stays in the list. That is the 'add wins' behaviour.

question: A like-counter is edited offline on several devices. Last-writer-wins ended at 81 against a true total of 140. Which representation fits?
options: A LWW-Register holding the number, with a replica-id tie-break
An OR-Set with one element per like, so that every concurrent like is kept as a separate tag
A PN-Counter: per-replica slots merged by max, so no increment is lost
A plain integer synced more often
explanation: Concurrent increments must all survive, which a per-replica counter merged by max guarantees (140 on every replica, 76 bytes per sync). A tie-break makes LWW converge but still discards concurrent increments.

question: One item is added and removed 1,000 times; the list shows one item but each sync ships 31,813 bytes. What is the cause?
options: The G-Counter slots grow by one byte per sync
Duplicated syncs make the merge store a second copy of each state it receives
OR-Set tombstones are never collected; compaction needs coordination
LWW timestamps grow without bound as more writes happen
explanation: Every remove keeps the observed tags as tombstones, so metadata grows while the visible value does not. Compaction is possible but needs agreement that every replica has seen the removes.

question: Why can a CRDT not enforce 'stock never goes below 0' across offline replicas?
options: CRDTs cannot represent negative numbers
Each replica decides locally; merged decrements can oversell the item
The merge is not commutative for counters, so replicas disagree about the stock level
Stock needs a wall clock, and CRDTs use Lamport clocks
explanation: Two replicas can each sell the last item without seeing the other, and merging both decrements gives -1. Global invariants need reservations or coordination; merge laws only guarantee convergence.

question: A leader takes 100 order writes per second with asynchronous replication, and the cross-region follower lags about 160 ms when the leader's region fails. Roughly how many acknowledged writes are lost?
options: about 1.6 writes
about 0 writes
about 16 writes
about 160 writes
explanation: Writes acknowledged within the replication lag never reached the survivor: 100/s x 0.16 s, in line with the lab's 16-17 lost writes. Majority-sync makes this zero by waiting for a follower before acknowledging.

question: One-way latencies are us-eu 40 ms, eu-ap 70 ms, us-ap 110 ms. With majority-sync, a write goes client -> leader -> nearest follower and back -> client. Ignoring jitter, which leader region minimises the worst region's commit latency?
options: us (worst region 300 ms)
eu (worst region 220 ms)
ap (worst region 360 ms)
eu (worst region 160 ms)
explanation: With the leader in eu the nearest follower is us (80 ms round trip): us users 160 ms, eu 80 ms, ap 220 ms. A leader in us makes ap users pay 110 ms each way plus the commit leg (300 ms).

question: Why can majority-sync lose no committed write when the whole leader region fails?
options: The leader flushes every write to its local disk before it acknowledges the client
A commit needs one follower, and the most up-to-date survivor becomes leader
Followers reject writes from a leader in another region
Clients resend every write after a failover
explanation: A committed write is on the leader plus at least one follower, and electing the most up-to-date survivor guarantees the new leader holds it. A disk flush on the failed region does not help when the region is gone.

question: What does a follower read in ap cost and buy compared with reading at the leader in eu?
options: A fresh value at local speed, because followers apply every write before the leader acknowledges it
About 2 ms locally instead of a leader round trip, but stale by up to the replication lag
Lower write latency, because reads stop competing with writes
Higher availability with no staleness, because it bypasses the leader
explanation: A local follower answers in ~2 ms but may be up to 103.6 ms behind (p99) in ap, while a leader read costs ~140 ms. Freshness at the leader also requires it to confirm it still leads.

question: You switch to a LAN-style election timeout (150-300 ms instead of 1-2 s) on the same WAN. RTO falls from 1,313 ms to 278 ms in the simulation. What is the main risk in production?
options: Lost acknowledged writes, because RPO rises above 0
Conflicting writes, because two leaders could accept writes for the same order at once
Slower writes, because every write waits for the election timer
False elections when WAN round trips plus jitter approach the timeout
explanation: The simulation does not model false elections, but on a real WAN a timeout close to RTT plus jitter triggers elections without failures. Majority-sync keeps RPO 0 either way.

question: Orders must never conflict and RPO must be 0. Multi-leader gave 140/127/113 ms writes but 434 conflicts. Where is multi-leader an acceptable choice?
options: For orders too, provided conflicts are resolved by a last-writer-wins rule on each order
For orders, once a region failure has made it the only option
For carts or counters with mergeable CRDT values, not for orders
Nowhere: multi-leader always loses acknowledged writes
explanation: Multi-leader writes are local and survive failures, but concurrent writes to one key conflict; that is fine only when values merge (lesson 18). LWW on orders would silently drop customers' writes.

question: The deployed leader sits in ap because the team launched there first. How should the leader region be chosen instead?
options: By measured, traffic-weighted p99 for today's users, kept true by a fitness test
By the region with the most servers, since that region can absorb the extra load of a failover
By whichever region launched first, to avoid a migration
By the region with the lowest average ping to the database vendor
explanation: Leader placement fixes every user's commit path, so it should follow measured latency weighted by where traffic comes from (eu in the lab). History is not evidence; a fitness test re-checks the choice as traffic shifts.

question: Traffic is us 50%, eu 35%, ap 15%, and the brief caps us and eu write p99 at 350 ms. What is wrong with this place_leader()?
options: It weights every region equally and ignores the per-region budget
It should use max() so the leader lands in the slowest region
It should rank leaders by p50, because p99 is too noisy to compare
It should always pick us, the region with the most traffic
explanation: Here it returns 'ap' (plain mean 286.7 ms), which breaks the 350 ms cap for us users (360 ms). Placement should first drop leaders that break a per-region cap, then minimise traffic-weighted p99: that picks 'us' (297.0 ms). Picking the busiest region by rule ignores everyone else's commit path.

question: A chaos experiment injects a fault that harms every faulted order. 80 orders run with a 25% cohort. How many customers are hurt without an abort rule, and with an abort after the first harmed order?
options: 80 without abort, 1 with abort
20 without abort, 0 with abort
20 without abort, 1 with abort
25 without abort, 1 with abort
explanation: The cohort is 25% of 80 = 20 orders, all harmed if the hypothesis is false; an abort rule stops injecting after the first harm. The lab saw the same pattern: 30 hurt at 50%, 6 at 10%, 1 with abort.

question: What is a chaos experiment's hypothesis about?
options: That the system will break in a visible way as soon as the planned fault is injected into it
That the fault injection tool works as configured
That no customer will notice the experiment
That the steady state continues in the experiment group as in the control group
explanation: The experiment tries to refute a claim about measurable normal behaviour (here: harmed orders = 0) under a real-world fault. It is a test of steady state, not a plan to break things.

question: What does a control group give you that the experiment group alone cannot?
options: A second chance to inject the same fault if the first run passes without any harm to customers
Extra traffic so the experiment finishes faster
A baseline under the same conditions, showing whether harm came from your fault
A place to inject the fault if the cohort is too small
explanation: If the control group is harmed too, the cause is not your fault, or the fault leaked beyond the cohort. Without it, you cannot tell your fault's effect from background problems.

question: Random single-node crashes held the hypothesis in 20 of 20 runs against the unhardened Raft, yet a fast rolling restart lost committed entries in 1 of 20. Why?
options: Rolling restarts take two of the three nodes down at once, which is more than a majority can ever tolerate
Random crashes were injected into the wrong cluster
The rolling restart used a different, buggier Raft build
The bug needs a lagging node to win right after restarting, which a rolling restart lines up
explanation: Independent random crashes rarely create the sequence the bug needs; an operational sequence like a quick rollout does. That is why incident sequences belong in the campaign alongside random faults.

question: Which number should an experiment's abort rule watch?
options: A five-minute aggregate error rate across all traffic, which smooths out noise
The CPU load of the fault-injection tool
The number of faults injected so far
The experiment group's steady-state metric, per request or order
explanation: An abort is only as fast as its signal: a per-order metric on the experiment group stops after the first harm, while a delayed aggregate lets harm accumulate. Counting faults says nothing about harm.

question: Waiting 20-30 ticks between nodes in the rolling restart made the unhardened Raft pass 20 of 20 seeds. What should the team conclude?
options: The slower rollout hides the bug; the election-restriction fix removes it
The bug is fixed, because the experiment no longer refutes the hypothesis
The experiment is broken, because it stopped finding the bug
Rolling restarts are unsafe and must be replaced by full restarts
explanation: An operational workaround changes the timing so the bug is no longer reached, but the code still has it; the code fix makes it impossible. Safety must not depend on timing.

question: A bounded experiment faults a 10% cohort of 60 orders and aborts after the first harmed order. What does it print?
code:
ABORT_AFTER, hurt, injected = 1, 0, 0
cohort = [o for o in range(60) if o % 10 == 0]  # 10% of 60 orders
for order in cohort:
    injected += 1
    hurt += 1  # the hypothesis is false: every faulted order is harmed
    if hurt >= ABORT_AFTER:
        break
print(injected, hurt, 60 - len(cohort))
explanation: The first cohort order is harmed, which meets ABORT_AFTER, so injection stops after 1 order; the other 54 orders form the control group. Without the break all 6 cohort orders would be harmed.

question: You want to test a fault in a cache shared by all orders. In earlier runs the control group showed harmed orders. What should you do?
options: Stop and redesign: the fault cannot be keyed to the cohort, so it leaks
Increase the cohort to 100% so the control group is no longer needed
Ignore the control group for this one, since the cache is shared by every order anyway
Raise the abort threshold so the experiment can finish
explanation: Faults on shared components (caches, global config, a region) leak into the control group, and harm there is the signal to stop. Dropping the control group removes the evidence rather than the risk.

question: This harness correctly refuted the saga hypothesis but hurt all 60 customers. Which change bounds it?
options: Fault only a stable 10% cohort, keep the rest as control, and stop after the first harm
Wrap inject() in try/except so a failing fault cannot crash the harness
Shuffle the orders first so the fault hits them in a random order
Count harmed orders only at the end, so one bad order cannot stop the run
explanation: The harness injects into every order, keeps no control group and never aborts, so harm scales with all traffic; the bounded version hurt 1 customer with the same verdict. Deferring the count is the opposite of an abort rule.

question: Why does breadth-first search return the shortest counterexample trace?
options: It visits states in order of distance from the start, so the first violation is closest
It collects every violating trace it finds, sorts them by length, and returns the shortest one at the end
It stops exploring a branch as soon as it becomes long
It only explores traces up to a fixed maximum length
explanation: BFS explores all states at depth k before depth k+1, so the first violating state found has the minimal number of steps. Depth bounds limit the search but do not by themselves make the result shortest.

question: Why does the VoteOnce invariant check a ghost log of votes instead of each node's votedFor?
options: votedFor is not hashable, so it cannot be stored in the visited set of explored states
Ghost variables are faster to check than real ones
votedFor is only set on the leader, not on voters
A restart erases votedFor, so an invariant over it cannot see the double vote
explanation: The bug is that a node forgets its vote after restarting; the ghost log keeps every vote ever cast and is never erased by crashes. Checking the cause (VoteOnce) finds the bug in 4 steps.

question: Raising MAX_TERM from 2 to 3 grew the fixed election model from 1,853 to 29,221 distinct states. By what factor did the state space grow?
options: about 1.6x
about 27.4x
about 15.8x
about 0.1x
explanation: 29,221 / 1,853 is about 15.8, the lab's 'x16 per extra term'. State explosion is why bounds must be small and stated with every claim.

question: Random simulation hit the election bug in 16 of 1,000 random walks. If each walk independently hits it with that probability, what is the chance that a CI run of 100 walks finds it?
options: about 80%
about 16%
about 100%
about 2%
explanation: The chance of at least one hit is 1 - (1 - 0.016)^100. Random walks are a cheap smoke test, but one run in five would still pass the buggy protocol, while BFS finds it every time.

question: BFS searches this state graph for the 'bad' state and rebuilds the trace from parents. What does it print?
options: s->a->c->bad
s->a->bad
s->b->bad
bad->b->s
explanation: BFS reaches 'bad' first through b at depth 2, before the longer path through a and c; the path is rebuilt backwards from parents and then reversed. A depth-first search might return the longer trace.

question: The history checker says 'not linearizable', but the store looks correct. The recorder is below. What is the likely problem?
code:
import time

def record(history, op, call):
    result = call()
    start = time.monotonic()
    end = time.monotonic()
    history.append((op, start, end, result))
    return result
options: time.monotonic() is not precise enough for history checking
The start time is taken after the request returns, so operations look shorter than they were
The checker needs the operations sorted by end time first
The result value should be recorded before the request is sent, because replies can arrive out of order
explanation: An operation's start must be recorded before the request is sent and its end after the reply; here both are taken after the call, so the interval shrinks and valid overlaps look like reorderings. Monotonic time is the right clock.

question: A pull request says votedFor need not be persisted, and three example tests pass. What should guard protocol changes like this before merge?
options: More example-based tests written by the reviewers
1,000 random simulation walks, which found the bug 16 times
Exhaustive model checking of the protocol model within stated bounds
Linearizability checks of production histories after release
explanation: BFS over every reachable state found a 7-step counterexample after 4,519 states, which example tests missed. Random walks give no guarantee, and history checking judges only runs that already happened.

question: What does a transactional outbox guarantee?
options: The event is stored in the same local transaction as the state change, then relayed at least once
The event is delivered exactly once to every consumer
The state change and every consumer's effect commit together in one distributed transaction across services
The relay publishes the event before the state change commits
explanation: Writing state and event together means neither exists without the other; the relay then publishes at least once, so consumers must still deduplicate. It is not a distributed transaction with the consumers.

question: You remove deduplication from the consumers and run with duplicate deliveries. Which rubric criterion fails?
options: One order and one charge per key: two orders created per key
Exactly-once effects: up to 2 emails per event and 14 revenue mismatches
Bounded queue: the queue grows above its committed bound
One trace per order: duplicates start new traces
explanation: Duplicated events now cause duplicated effects, which is exactly what the exactly-once-effects check measures. Order creation is guarded by the gateway's idempotency keys, which were not changed.

question: The gateway forgets idempotency keys and acknowledgements are lost. Which criteria fail?
options: Only the money invariant, because charges are doubled
Only bounded queue, because the clients' retries pile up in the gateway queue until it overflows
None, because consumers deduplicate every event
One order and one charge per key, and exactly-once effects (2 orders created for a key)
explanation: Client retries now create a second order for the same key (max created 2), and the exactly-once-effects check also fails (up to 2 emails per event); charges stay at 1 per key, so the money invariant is not what breaks. Consumer dedup works per event id, so it cannot undo a second order.

question: An idempotent email consumer receives these events. How many emails does it send?
explanation: The duplicate e1 is skipped, but e2 has a new event id for the same order, so a second email goes out. That is why outbox events must be written only when state actually changed: a re-run that emits a new event defeats consumer dedup.

question: The gateway's queue bound stays at 1 until the first config change commits through Raft. Why not apply the newest proposed value right away?
options: Proposed values are encrypted until they commit
A proposal may never commit, e.g. after a leader crash; only committed, versioned config is safe
The gateway is unable to read the Raft log at all until the very first entry has been committed by a majority
Applying a proposal would double the queue bound
explanation: A proposed entry can be lost if the leader crashes before a majority stores it; acting on it could apply a value the cluster never agreed on. Versions also stop a stale leader or retry from applying an older value.

question: The local model's summary says the relay-crash experiment 'held=no' and that the build is not safe to release. What happens?
options: Code marks the claim WRONG and the scorecard decides; the model never decides
The release is blocked, because any negative claim must be investigated first
The scorecard is recomputed with the model's verdict as an extra criterion
The experiment is re-run until the model and the code agree
explanation: The model only explains; checks.py computes each criterion from the system's own data and flags model claims that disagree. Its release verdict is ignored by design.

question: Where does the capstone shed load during a flash-sale burst, and why there?
options: In the payments service, so that only orders which have not been paid yet are dropped
In the email consumer, since emails are the least important effect
At admission in the gateway, with 503 + Retry-After, before any saga work starts
Nowhere: the outbox absorbs any burst, so no shedding is needed
explanation: Refusing work before the saga starts costs almost nothing and keeps the queue under its committed bound (ADR shed at admission). Dropping work mid-saga would leave half-finished orders needing compensation.
